value.overview: The Dark-billed Cuckoo (Coccyzus melacoryphus) is a medium-sized cuckoo of South America and the Galápagos Islands. It is usually associated with lowland woodland, forest edges, scrub, gallery forest, second growth, plantations, and mangroves. Most individuals are quiet and secretive, often remaining concealed in dense vegetation. Its deep, descending calls may reveal its presence before the bird is seen. In Costa Rica, it is an accidental and very rarely recorded visitor rather than a regular species.
value.classification: The Dark-billed Cuckoo belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, and the genus Coccyzus. It is a New World cuckoo and is not an obligate brood parasite.
value.identification: This cuckoo has brownish-gray upperparts, a gray crown, pale buff underparts, and a distinct dark bill. A dark mask extends through the eye, which may show a yellowish or orange-yellow eye-ring. The long, dark tail has conspicuous white markings on the underside and tips. Juveniles are duller and browner. It is often detected by its low, resonant, descending series of guttural or buzzing notes.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs widely across tropical and subtropical South America, from Venezuela and Colombia south through Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, and Argentina, and also inhabits the Galápagos Islands. It uses tropical deciduous and gallery forests, mature secondary growth, forest edges, scrub, plantations, riparian vegetation, and mangroves, mainly in lowlands. In Costa Rica it is listed as accidental, with very few accepted records; documented occurrences include the southern Pacific region, such as Puntarenas, and do not indicate an established population.
value.migrationStatus: Migration varies geographically. Populations in southern Brazil, Uruguay, and Argentina move north during the austral winter, while some northern populations are resident or make seasonal movements. In Costa Rica, the species is an accidental vagrant, not a regular seasonal migrant, and there is no reliable evidence of regular passage, wintering, or breeding there.
value.breeding: Dark-billed Cuckoos build a simple, shallow platform or cup of sticks in a tree or shrub. Clutches usually contain two or three greenish-blue eggs, although larger clutches have been reported in Argentina. Incubation begins before the clutch is complete, so hatching can be asynchronous and young may differ in size. The species breeds in parts of South America and the Galápagos, but there is no reliable evidence that it breeds in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects, including caterpillars, grasshoppers, and other terrestrial arthropods. It may also take other invertebrates and some fruit, particularly when seasonal insect supplies are reduced. The bird usually forages alone or in pairs, moving deliberately through foliage, shrubs, woodland edges, and other dense vegetation. In northeastern Brazil, recent research found Lepidoptera and Orthoptera to be especially important prey during the breeding season.
value.behavior: This is a secretive, generally solitary cuckoo that spends much of its time within vegetation and may be easier to hear than see. It moves through branches and undergrowth in a deliberate manner and can remain motionless when approached. Its calls are deep, resonant, and sometimes descending or buzzing. Seasonal movements are linked partly to breeding and food availability. Nest building and parental care are carried out by the adults, rather than relying on obligatory brood parasitism.

conservation.populationTrend: Stable globally, although the total population size is not well quantified.
